newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS-Malaysia intervenes to stem ringgit's fall.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Malaysia intervenes to stem ringgit's fall.

text.p: The Malaysian central bank on Wednesday intervened in the foreign exchange market after the ringgit fell to a three-month low against the U.S. dollar, dealers said.
"The central bank was acting through some large Malaysian banks. The intention seems to just slow the ringgit's fall, not stop it," said a dealer with a large Malaysian bank.
The central Bank Negara Malaysia came into the market after 0230 GMT to sell an estimated $100-200 million to stop the ringgit's fall beyond 2.5120 per dollar, they said.
There was no confirmation from Bank Negara, which does not usually comment on its market intervention operations.
Some dealers even said it may not have been central bank intervention at all. "It could have just been corporate selling," said a dealer with a foreign bank in Malaysia.

But, most dealers, including those from banks who act as agents for Bank Negara, said the central bank was in the market and its selling lasted until the ringgit came down to 2.5100, with the bulk of transactions done around 2.5110.
Bank Negara's action triggered an all-round halt to ringgit selling and helped the Malaysian unit recover to around 2.5055/65 by 0400 GMT, the dealers said.
Support from the central bank also brought in Malaysian exporters, who had wanted a strong U.S. unit when selling their dollars, dealers said.
"Speculators who had been buying dollar/ringgit this morning also started squaring up as soon as they heard selling from Kuala Lumpur side," said a dealer with another Malaysian bank.
"This exaggerated the volumes (after the intervention)," he said.
However, the strength of the dollar against the majors would not allow a major correction in dollar/ringgit, which has risen nearly 200 points in the past two days, dealers said.
In the morning, dollar/ringgit broke through 2.51 per dollar, triggering stop-loss selling, and the rinnggit was expected to fall further as result.
The Malaysian unit, which had been on the rise since early January thanks to strong economic fundamentals and high interest rates, has fallen sharply this week.

A U.S. hedge fund, squaring up a large three-month position in the ringgit, was said to be mainly responsible for the Malaysian currency's latest decline. The position is estimated to be in excess of two billion ringgit.
In addition, dealers said the strength of the U.S. dollar against the yen and other major currencies was also weakening regional currencies such as the ringgit.
The Malaysian unit has gained up to 2.2 percent this year before settling in a wide range of 2.4750-2.4900 per dollar. It broke out of this range on Monday on selling by the hedge fund.
"With the assumed presence of Bank Negara, there should be strong resistance at the 2.51 level," said a dealer with a European bank in Singapore.

A dealer with a Malaysian bank said the ringgit's fall was not an attack on the currency, but just squaring of positions by the hedge fund and covering of long ringgit holdings against the Singapore dollar.
"Once the market is done with covering long positions, there should be a recovery in the ringgit. Long-term sentiment is still in favour of the ringgit," the dealer said.
-- Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603-230 7509)
